messages.subject: request for help with DISTANCE
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am a beginner in using DISTANCE and am in the process of analyzing some
data on butterflies in Assam, northeastern India.

Could someone help me with the following questions:

a) Does the calculation for g(0) and f(0) have to be separate for each
stratum?, i.e. do I have to run separate analyses for each stratum?

b) I am involved in a multi-species survey, and thus would like to know how
I calculate density for each species.

Sorry for cross-posting.
Looking forward to some advice.

Thanks,
Maan

Maan Barua
Kaziranga National Park
Assam, India

messages.body_plain:
Dear all!
  We are trying to find the population density of an endemic species, the Cyprus moufflon.
  We have our data separated in two strata; forest core and forest edge. The data was collected using 20 line transects and the perpendicular distance of the animals was estimated using a laser machine. Our problem is that we cannot find the correct density (the numbers are too low); the data is separated into region (forest core and forest edge), Line transect (label), Line transect (length), Observation (perpendicular distance) and 4 columns of observations (numbers of males, females, youngs and newborns). We use the uniform parameter with cosine adjustment (not sure if this is correct)

  Any help would be greatly appreciated.

  Thanks

messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I have asked this question previously, but it has been awhile so =
I=20
thought I'd ask again.

I have distance sampling data from avian point count surveys in areas=20
treated by prescribed fire and untreated areas.  I would like to relate=20=

habitat characteristics at the level of the point count to density=20
estimates at the point count. Obviously, I would need to pool data to=20
estimate a detection function to get the density estimates for each=20
individual point count.  It is my understanding that there are a variety =
of=20
statistical issues associated with conducting this type of analysis.=20=20=

I know there are papers by Royle addressing this issue, but I'm confused=20=

about whether the methods suggested by Royle in Ecology 2004 are=20
appropriate for my data or if there are other methods that are more=20
appropriate.

Perhaps this analysis is not as complicated as I was lead to believe?

Any help on the matter would be appreciated.

Thanks,

messages.subject: Re: modeling density estimates
messages.body_plain:
I thought I answered this one or one like it awhile back,  The method
proposed by Royle et al would work for what you want to do.  The only
statistical issue is in coping with the uncertainty associated with
estimation of the detection probability in the evaluation of the density
affect.  However, in your case this is relatively straightforward as
long as you estimate detection probability separately for the treatment
(fire) and control areas.  Then you can construct 2 independent
estimates of D with std errors that incorporate both variation due to
sampling and estimation of detection probability.  You can construct an
approximate z-test as (Dfire - Dcontrol)/sqrt(var(Dfire) +
var(Dcontrol)).  If your df are small you may want to use the
Satterthwaite approximation and construct a pooled df and use a t-test
in evaluating the hypothesis.  Or if you prefer, you can estimate the
effect size as Dfire-Dcontrol and its std error is simply
sqrt(var(Dfire) + var(Dcontrol)).  If the individual cvs are large then
you may want to use the log normal approach instead rather than the
normality assumption.  It becomes trickier if you have a common
detection function but even than can be handled in the case of
trt-control.  What gets messier is more than one level for the treatment
or multiple covariate effects.  That is where the method proposed by
Royle et al will be better and frames the analysis in a model selection
approach with a likelihood for abundance as well as detection.  There is
a considerable amount of work being done on this subject and eventuallly
software will follow.  For the time being what I've described above may
work for your situation.

regards --jeff

messages.body_plain:

think this is the problem in your case.  If you can't figure it out from the
above then send me a copy of your project (File | Export as zip).

 - Len

messages.subject: Re: Comparing densities obtained from different models
messages.subject_clean: Comparing densities obtained from different models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Harriet, List,

There should be no problem at all in comparing two independent estimates=20
with different detection function models, given that the distance=20
sampling assumptions hold in both instances. Since each estimate is then=20
an unbiased estimate (with a precision measure associated with it), and=20
these are independent, the comparison is straightforward.

As you say, given that the same data is used, a negative exponential=20
model tends to lead to higher estimates than the half normal say. But=20
that in itself is not an issue. What is an issue, and one that maybe you=20
need to think about, is why did you get the negative exponential to be=20
selected by AIC in the first place. I guess in most cases in which the=20
negative exponential is selected based on AIC it is so because there was=20
a problem in the data rather than it representing the true detection=20
function.

Do you have spiked data? If so, why are the data spiked? Is there an=20
assumption violation going on? Do you have too many 0 distances in your=20
data?

Your solution to force the same model to these 2 data sets is not=20
reasonable, because you do not need at all to have the same model to=20
make proper comparisons. In fact, in many cases you will have different=20
models across different species, but that just tells you that these=20
species have different detection functions. Fitting the same model, say=20
the half normal, will probably mean the kudu estimates become lower, but=20
it will not mean that the new estimate is better than the old one. What=20
you need to do first is to understand  why the  data was spiked to=20
beguin with, to then be able to act accordingly.

Hope this helps,

Tiago

messages.body_plain:
The form of model fitted to your data, consequently the adjustment terms=20
employed is a function of the data collected. It will not be a matter of=20
fitting a single model to your data, but rather, you will fit a set of=20
models to your data, and use model selection procedures, such as AIC to=20
select the most appropriate model from among the models you fit to your=20
data. I suggest you consult the following sections of Buckland et al.=20
(2001): Introduction to distance sampling: Section 2.5 (some analysis=20
guidelines) and Section 4.6 (model selection of line transect data).

messages.subject: Re: combination?
messages.body_plain:
Hi CK,

Yes, you can do this quite easily.  If you want to estimate density/abundance
in the two months separately, but also try having a pooled detection function
by month you should set up month as the stratum layer, with transects within
stratum.  You could then do analyses with detection function pooled across
months, detection function stratified by month, or even month as a factor
covariate in the MCDS engine.  Assuming no other problems in the detection
function, etc, then the analysis with the lowest AIC is the one you might
prefer.

I'm sure this has been discussed on the list before -- try searching the
archives for more details if you need them.  Otherwise email me (not the list)
and I can explain more (we could then post a summary of our discussion to the
list if that seems useful).

Hope this helps.

 - Len

messages.subject: Re: Ungulate data set
messages.body_plain:
Kausik,

Here's how I'd do it:

Put a field (column) in the observation data layer called "species".  Then,
for each observation, you put the species code in this column, along with
the distances in the Perp distance column, the cluster size in the Cluster
size column, etc.

Now, to analyze data for just one species, create a new analysis, and a new
data filter for that analysis, and then in the Data selection tab of the
Data Filter Properties, click on "+" to add a new selection criterion, and
under "Layer Type" choose observation and under "Selection criteria" type
something like
Species = "Elephant"
or whatever species code it is you want to select out.

You can set up one data filter for each species you want to analyze, and use
this data filter for lots of analyses on this species using, for example,
different model definitions that define alternative detection function
models.

There are several ways you could approach the analysis for all ungulates.

The easiest, but probably not the best, is to run an analysis of all the
data pooled - that is with no data filter selection criteria.  This should
give you a more-or-less unbiased estiamte of total density - you're relying
on the pooling robustness property of the detection function estimator,
which means there should be little bias in the overall density estimate even
if you pool together groups (in this case species) with rather different
detection functions.

If the animals do have very different detection functions, the above will
not work (you will get bad bias).  Also, precision might be poor.  So, a
second approach (if you have enough data) would be to post-stratify by
species, or use species as a covariate in an MCDS analysis.

The only downside of this is that you might already in your previous by-
species analyses, have selected different key functions (+ adjustments) for
the different species, and perhaps you want to keep this in the combined
analysis.  If so, the only way I can think of is to manually sum the
densities from each of the by-species analyses done previously.
Unfortunately, to get a variance estimate, some hand calculations are then
required, as outlined in sections 3.6.1 and 3.7.1 of Introduction to
Distance Sampling.  If the thought of some hand-calculating seems too much,
then possible stick with one of the strategies outlined in the previous 2
paragraphs instead!

Hope this helps,

 - Len Thomas
